summary: Defines terms used in performance benchmarking of frame relay switching devices and in reporting test results, so that measurements are described consistently.

eli5.summary: It is a dictionary of words for measuring how fast a data-moving machine is, so everyone means the same thing.

subtitle: A dictionary for measuring frame relay network performance.

tldr.problem: When testing frame relay switches and networks, vendors and operators need a consistent way to define and report performance measurements so results are comparable.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3133 defines terminology for frame relay switching devices, extending benchmarking terminology from earlier RFCs (1242, 1944, 2285) with frame relay-specific concepts and performance metrics.
tldr.outcome: The document provides a common vocabulary for benchmarking methodology work by the BMWG (Benchmarking Methodology Working Group), enabling standardized performance testing.

today: Frame relay has declined significantly in deployment since this RFC was published in 2001, as Ethernet and IP-based services have taken over its role. However, the terminology and methodology established here remains relevant for any benchmarking work involving frame relay legacy networks and provides a foundational model for benchmarking other switching technologies.

sections.title: Frame Relay and Benchmarking Terminology
sections.content: Frame relay is a high-performance packet-switching technology more efficient than X.25, designed to handle bursty communications with rapidly changing bandwidth requirements. This RFC extends the benchmarking terminology already defined in RFCs 1242, 1944 and 2285 with terms specific to frame relay switching devices. The document is a product of the Benchmarking Methodology Working Group (BMWG) of the IETF, which produces two classes of documents: Terminology documents that define benchmarks and related terms, and Methodology documents that specify how to collect those benchmarks. RFC 3133 provides the terminology needed to measure frame relay performance consistently.
sections.eli5: Frame relay is a mail-sorting machine for networks. This document is the glossary everyone uses when measuring how fast and reliable it is.

sections.title: Core Frame Relay Concepts
sections.content:
Frame relay terminology begins with several foundational concepts. A Data Link Connection Identifier (DLCI) is a unique number identifying a particular connection endpoint in a frame relay network; it has local significance only to that channel. Frame relay connects DTEs (Data Terminal Equipment, such as routers) to DCEs (Data Communications Equipment, the switches themselves). An access channel is the user connection across which frame relay data travels; it can be unchannelized (the entire T1 or E1 line is one channel) or channelized (multiple time slots on a line). The Committed Information Rate (CIR) is the data rate the network guarantees it will maintain between service locations. The Committed Burst Size (Bc) is the maximum amount of data the network agrees to transfer during a time interval Tc (Committed Rate Measurement Interval). The Excess Burst Size (Be) is additional data beyond Bc that the network will attempt to deliver with lower probability, marked as discard eligible.

Frame relay headers contain several important bits and fields. The FECN (Forward Explicit Congestion Notification) bit signals congestion in the forward direction. The BECN (Backward Explicit Congestion Notification) bit signals congestion in the reverse direction. The DE (Discard Eligible) bit marks frames that may be discarded if congestion occurs. The FCS (Frame Check Sequence) is a 16-bit checksum detecting errors. Frames consist of opening and closing flags, a header, user data (up to 1600 octets), and the FCS.
sections.eli5: Frame relay has connection numbers (DLCIs) for each link, guaranteed speeds (CIR), and markers on frames saying "if congested, you can throw this away" (DE bit). The frame has a checksum so you know if it got corrupted.

sections.title: Service Availability and Network Events
sections.content: To measure frame relay network health, the document defines service availability parameters that report the operational readiness of virtual connections. Service outages are any event interrupting frame relay traffic. Two types are differentiated: fault outages from network defects (tracked by service availability parameters) and excluded outages from faults beyond network control or scheduled maintenance. Physical layer problems are tracked separately; for example, an AIS (Alarm Indication Signal) is an all-ones frame transmitted when a defect is detected, LOS (Loss of Signal) means no signal transitions are occurring, LOF (Loss of Frame) is when an out-of-frame condition persists, and OOF (Out of Frame) means the receiver detected framing errors. Each of these causes loss of information in frames being transported. Interworking with ATM is also addressed: Network Interworking (FRF.5) maps protocols between frame relay and ATM, while Service Interworking (FRF.8) encapsulates one protocol's service over another's layer.
sections.eli5: Service availability measures are ways to track if the mail-sorting machine is working. Different types of outages (real failures versus maintenance) are tracked separately. Sometimes frame relay connects to ATM networks, which needs translation.

sections.title: Performance Metrics for Frame Delivery
sections.content:
The document defines several key performance metrics for measuring frame relay effectiveness. Data Delivery Ratio (DDR) is the ratio of successfully delivered payload octets to payload octets offered, showing the network's effectiveness at transporting data. It can be reported overall or separately for traffic within the CIR and traffic in excess of CIR. Frame Delivery Ratio (FDR) similarly measures successful frames received versus attempted frames transmitted, again with variants for committed and excess traffic.

Frame Loss Ratio (FLR) specifically measures frames lost at the CIR level: it is 1 minus the ratio of frames delivered to frames offered within the committed rate. Frame Discard Ratio (FDR) measures frames discarded due to errors (including frames too long or short, invalid DLCIs, FCS failures). Frame Excess Ratio (FXR) measures frames treated as excess traffic—those sent with more than Bc bits in interval Tc or marked with DE=1. Frame Error Ratio (FER) measures frames containing payload errors divided by total frames transmitted.

These metrics may not always reflect true application performance. For example, loss of a small acknowledgement frame can cause retransmission of many data frames, making the delivery ratio appear good while user experience is poor. Measurements must account for frame sizes and application requirements.
sections.eli5: Performance metrics count how many messages got through and how many were lost or damaged. Different metrics focus on different things: delivery of data (DDR), delivery of frames (FDR), lost frames (FLR), discarded frames, frames sent as extra traffic (FXR), and corrupted frames. But losing a single small message might be worse than losing a big one, so the numbers don't tell the whole story.

sections.title: Measurement Conventions and Standards References
sections.content: For consistent metric computation, RFC 3133 specifies formal mathematical notation. The summation notation sum {i=1 to N} A_i denotes the sum of N instances of observable A, and max {i=1 to N} A_i and min {i=1 to N} A_i denote maximum or minimum. Frame relay benchmarking terminology follows the definition template established in RFC 1242, with each term having a formal definition, discussion section explaining its application and measurement restrictions, and specification reference. The document references and builds upon three prior benchmarking RFCs: RFC 1242 (general network interconnect device terminology), RFC 1944 (network interconnect device methodology), and RFC 2285 (LAN switching device terminology). All metrics are defined with their measurement units (many are dimensionless ratios, but some include time or octets). This foundation allows the BMWG's complementary methodology documents to specify procedures for collecting these benchmarks from frame relay switching devices in standardized ways.
sections.eli5: The document uses mathematical notation to define how to calculate metrics, so researchers follow the same process. It references three earlier documents that set up the rules for testing network machines, so frame relay metrics fit into a consistent system.
